vignette:
He is a 46-year-old South Eastern Asian man who comes across as steady and careful in the way he speaks, as if he has learned to measure every word before it leaves him. He is married, works as a software engineer, and describes himself as someone who has always preferred structure, logic, and systems that behave predictably. Before the war, he thought of himself as disciplined but not especially rigid. Since the combat exposure, he notices that his life has narrowed around safety, routines, and the constant effort to keep his body from being surprised.

He does not begin his story with fear. He begins with the work itself: the months of deployments, the exhaustion, the long stretches of alertness that made sleep feel more like a lapse than a rest. He remembers the first time a roadside blast threw dust over the convoy and the air changed shape around him. In the moment, he says, there was no time for feeling. There was training, shouting, injury, the instinct to move, to help, to look for the next threat. What stayed with him afterward was not the single event but the accumulation of it: the smell of burned metal, the sudden silence after gunfire, the way a helmet rolling across the ground could sound like something alive.

He returned home physically intact, but it took him months to understand that nothing in him had truly come back. At first he tried to resume ordinary life as if he could step back into it seamlessly. He returned to his software engineering job and sat in meetings with the same focused expression he had always used when debugging code. Coworkers saw him as quiet and efficient. He could still write elegant solutions and handle complex problems, but he describes spending most of that time with one part of his mind elsewhere, scanning exits, cataloging noises, noting who was behind him. He begins every workday by choosing a seat facing the door. If someone drops a binder or a chair scrapes the floor unexpectedly, his whole body jerks before he can think.

His sleep was the first thing to unravel. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes a few hours later with his heart racing, convinced for a moment that he is back in the field. Sometimes he wakes from the same dream: a dark road, headlights in the distance, the sense that something is about to happen and there is nowhere to go. He lies still beside his wife, listening to her breathing, and waits for the room to become recognizable again. On worse nights he gets up and checks the locks, then checks them again. He keeps his phone charged beside the bed and leaves a light on in the hallway, though he feels ashamed of how much these rituals matter to him.

He tries not to talk about the war, but the memories enter without invitation. A siren on the street can pull him back so suddenly that he has to grip a countertop until the moment passes. The smell of diesel, burning trash, or rain on hot pavement can bring back images he does not want to hold: bodies in the dust, a medic shouting, his own hands shaking as he pressed on a wound. He says the memories are not like stories but like intrusions, arriving with the force of something happening now. When that happens, he becomes distant and hard to reach. His wife tells him he looks “far away,” and he hates that she can see it. He still loves her, but he finds himself unable to explain what is happening inside him, and that distance makes him feel guilty and alone.

He has become more irritable, especially at home, where he is least able to hide the strain. He startles when his children run toward him too quickly or when the television is turned up unexpectedly. He snaps over small things and immediately regrets it, often retreating into silence afterward. He notices that he avoids news about war, action films, crowded public events, and even neighborhood gatherings that might include fireworks. He has turned down invitations he once would have accepted. He no longer drives on certain highways because the sight of barriers and debris can make his chest tighten. He chooses routes carefully, as if planning his commute is a way of managing the past.

Underneath all of this is a persistent sense that he is not fully present in his own life. He describes feeling detached from his family at times, as though he is watching himself from a distance. There are moments when he cannot access ordinary warmth or joy, even when he wants to. He still functions, still pays attention to deadlines, still fixes problems at work, but he does so with effort and a kind of inner bracing. He worries that if he relaxes, something terrible will happen. The war is over, but his body has not received the message, and he lives in the ongoing effort to keep the past from breaking into the present.
